paper_metadata.title: Autocallable Options Pricing with Integration-Based Exponential Amplitude Loading

summary: The paper presents a gate-based quantum algorithm for pricing a single-asset autocallable option using IQAE and integration-based exponential amplitude loading. It reports simulator-based experiments up to 33 logical qubits on Classiq, Nvidia, and LEONARDO/Cirq, and a ~50x reduction in payoff-component T-depth relative to the prior integration-based method, but no real-hardware advantage over classical baselines is demonstrated.

experiments.description: End-to-end gate-based quantum circuit for pricing a single-asset autocallable option, validated via simulation on Classiq/Nvidia/LEONARDO with scalability tests over Gaussian discretization and arithmetic precision.

algorithm.variant: Autocallable option pricing with integration-based exponential amplitude loading and IQAE
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) with target confidence level; paper sets total estimation error ϵ=0.001 and α=0.002 for validation runs
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Not reported; circuit synthesized from problem parameters

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Gaussian distributions loaded per time step into registers; log-returns accumulated in an arithmetic register; binary conditions checked with comparators; payoff encoded into target-qubit amplitude via controlled Ry and integration-based exponential amplitude loading
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate expected discounted payoff of an autocallable option, with payoff composed of mutually exclusive binary payouts and a knock-in put component
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Path-dependent conditions handled by comparators and indicator registers; barrier-crossing and binary-trigger exclusivity enforced by control logic; payoff rescaled to [0,1] for amplitude estimation

problem_instance.description: Single-asset autocallable option with 3 time steps and 2 binary options expiring at the first two monitoring points; includes a short knock-in put at maturity

dataset_specification.description: Model parameters given in Table II; no market dataset specified

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Gaussian discretization of log-returns; arithmetic precision varied in classical benchmark models; quantum circuit synthesized under accuracy constraints
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparison against classical Monte Carlo, Monte Carlo with same Gaussian discretization, closed form with same discretization, and closed form with discretization plus fixed-point precision; simulator executions for selected qubit/precision settings; convergence illustrated in Figures 3 and 4

hardware.transpilation_target: Classiq synthesized gate-based circuit optimized for width

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical benchmark models built to match quantum discretization and arithmetic precision; parameters from Table II
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: IQAE used to estimate target-qubit probability; payoff rescaling from amplitude domain back to monetary payoff

speedup_claims.conditions: using quantum amplitude estimation; query complexity O(1/epsilon) versus classical O(1/epsilon^2)
speedup_claims.caveats: This is the standard QAE asymptotic advantage, not an empirical hardware demonstration.

speedup_claims.caveats: Applies to the payoff component / amplitude-loading subroutine, not the full end-to-end circuit.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/ϵ) query complexity for amplitude estimation; full T-depth analyzed as Dtot = (1 + 2NIQAE) · (max (DG + Darith, Dexp) + DAL)
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: ~50x reduction in T-depth for payoff component relative to prior integration-based method in a relevant setting; paper also compares favorably to QSP-based approach

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 33 logical qubits reported for simulator executions; IQAE with total estimation error 0.001 and alpha 0.002; T-depth analysis gives ~50x reduction in payoff-component T-depth relative to prior method, but no end-to-end hardware advantage demonstrated
limiting_factors: quadratic speedup only via amplitude estimation
large circuit width/depth even for small instances
classical baselines used for comparison remain practical
paper reports symbolic T-depth improvements but not full-circuit runtime advantage

notes: 33 qubits is explicitly stated for experiments up to 33 qubits on LEONARDO.
Hardware is simulator-based; no real QPU used.
The paper reports T-depth improvements and a symbolic T-depth formula, but not a single absolute full-circuit depth for the experiment.
The paper presents a gate-based quantum algorithm and simulator validation, but does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage over classical methods.
Classical benchmarking is used to validate convergence, not to show quantum superiority.
